title: Lost for three days (Luke 2:41–52)
hook: twelve-year-old Jesus stays in the Temple and asks why they didn't know he'd be in his Father's house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, and a family running for Egypt. Your line was: the holy family were refugees. Week five starts now: the beginning. Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.` → `WEEK FIVE: THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: A crowded market. A parent turns around, and the child isn't there. The stomach drops. Every second becomes an hour. Now stretch that to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph walked to Jerusalem for the Passover, in a big crowd of relatives and neighbors. When Jesus is twelve, they start home, and assume he's somewhere in the caravan with the cousins. A whole day's walk later, they realize he isn't. They turn around. They search Jerusalem. One day. Two. Three. Today, Luke's story of Jesus at twelve.
screen: `YOU TURN AROUND. HE'S GONE.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `ONE DAY. TWO. THREE.`

segments.voice: Here's where they find him, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. And a twelve-year-old boy from a village is sitting among them, listening and asking questions, and Luke says everyone was astonished at how he understood and how he answered. Mary says what a frightened parent says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Sorrowing. Three days of it. And his answer is the first thing Jesus ever says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" Here's a detail worth knowing. In Luke's Greek, the phrase is short and open: literally, in the things of my Father. Older English Bibles say my father's business. Some newer ones say my Father's house. Both are possible. Either way, he's saying: I'm where I belong. Luke adds, honestly, that they didn't understand what he meant. Even Mary. And then he goes home with them, and is obedient to them, and Mary keeps all these things in her heart, the same words Luke used after the shepherds. Catholics hold this story in two places at once. It's the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary: the finding in the Temple, a joy. And it's one of the seven sorrows of Mary: three days of searching. Notice where they found him. Not playing, not lost and crying. Asking questions. In this story, questions aren't the opposite of faith. The first time we meet Jesus as more than a baby, that's what he's doing.
screen: `SITTING AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `THY FATHER AND I HAVE SOUGHT THEE.` · `IN THE THINGS OF MY FATHER.` · `A JOY AND A SORROW.` · then, large: `THEY FOUND HIM ASKING QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for today's two-minute sit. Think of a time you lost someone. Maybe for a few minutes in a crowd. Maybe for years, to a falling-out. Maybe for good. Let yourself remember what the searching felt like. Don't hurry past it. Then, if they were found, remember that moment too. If they weren't, just hold them gently. If you pray, you can bring them to God. The bell holds the time.
doctors. The teachers of the Law in the Temple, where the boy Jesus sat listening and asking questions.
Your line: they found him asking questions. Today, ask one real question about something you've always just accepted, and listen to the answer. Day twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics meditate on this story as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the Finding in the Temple, and as one of the Seven Sorrows of Mary; it is read on the feast of the Holy Family.

original.note: Greek: in the things of my Father. it can mean his house or his business; translations differ.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kid who wandered off.
what it means: the first words of Jesus in Luke: I'm where I belong, in the things of my Father, found asking questions.
what a scholar hears: en tois tou patros mou, ambiguous between house and affairs; three days foreshadowing the three days before Easter.
